provenance: Content-pattern fingerprints are the ones documented publicly for the named shell families (c99/r57/FilesMan/b374k/WSO write-ups and the PHP Malware Finder project, github.com/jvoisin/php-malware-finder) and for classic PHP backdoor idioms (request-superglobal eval/assert, preg_replace /e, base64/gzinflate eval chains). Filename IOCs are the canonical names those shells ship under. hashes_sha256 is INTENTIONALLY EMPTY in this release: no published webshell-hash list could be fetched with verifiable provenance at build time, and the project's honesty doctrine forbids shipping unverifiable indicator data. Detection is patterns + filenames + heuristics only.

filename_iocs.name: wso.php
filename_iocs.note: canonical WSO (Web Shell by Orb) filename

filename_iocs.name: x.php
filename_iocs.note: single-letter PHP filename, a common dropper name

filename_iocs.name: 1.php
filename_iocs.note: single-digit PHP filename, a common dropper name

content_patterns.note: eval() of raw request input — unambiguous backdoor idiom
assert() of raw request input (China Chopper-style one-liner)
eval() of a decode/decompress chain — classic obfuscated payload delivery
request input fed straight into base64_decode — dropper idiom
preg_replace /e modifier (removed in PHP 7) — code execution by regex, common in older shells
eval() usage — appears in some legitimate libraries; review, do not panic

remote_note: Remote mode is indicative, not conclusive: a 200 on one of these paths means a file with a known shell name answers in public. It can be a honeypot, a scanner artifact, or a coincidence — and a compromised site usually shows nothing here at all. Confirm with the local hunt on the server before concluding anything.
